data.claim: The server never rechecks the installed package; a skew refusal carries merge-main/upgrade advice and no restart instruction, the only restart note is a once-only footer on successful calls
data.falsifier: A refused write on a server with installed>running already tells the user to reconnect
data.mechanism: Server imports code once; _call_api REFUSED branch returns the plain SkewRefused text before footers run
data.probe_output: refusal text is the generic skew message (see test_upgrade_running_server body); no restart_required meta
data.question: Why does a long-lived MCP server refuse writes after an upgrade, and with what message?

evidence.note: research note recorded, CONFIRMED by reading _call_api and test_upgrade_running_server
ddflow rule list consulted via brief; no rule conflicts (surfaces->api layering respected, no subprocess, new knob has manifest fragment, new module under 20KB)
commit ec7bf9ac; 12 new tests in tests/test_mcp_on_upgrade.py plus 1417 focused tests pass

chunk_findings.detail: `footer()` returns the restart note without ever consulting `f["reexec"]`, while `refusal()` explicitly guards on it (`if f is None or not f["reexec"]: return None`, with the comment "nothing newer is installed: a restart would not help"). Given a server running 0.2.1 whose project log was written by 0.2.3 but where nothing newer than 0.2.1 is installed locally (e.g. the writer used a different checkout/install), `stale_server_facts` returns a non-`None` dict with `reexec == False` — the exact state `refusal()` treats as "not explained by staleness". `footer()` falls through the `mode == "reexec" and can_reexec(f)` branch (false, because `reexec` is false), sets `srv._stale_said = True` and returns `note(f)`, which instructs the user to "restart the server ... to pick up the upgrade". No upgrade is installed, so reconnecting re-runs the same code, the same skew remains, and — because `_stale_said` is now latched — the user is never told anything again. The advice is exactly the kind of dead-end the change is meant to eliminate; `footer()` should suppress the note (or use non-clamping wording) when `f["reexec"]` is false.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp_upgrade.py `footer()`

chunk_findings.detail: `execute()` serialises `"called_from": str(srv.called_from)`. When `srv.called_from` is `None` this writes the literal string `"None"`, and `called_from()` decodes it as `Path(value) if value else None` — `"None"` is truthy, so the re-exec'd process gets `Path("None")` instead of `None`. The `-> Path | None` return type and the `if value else None` guard show `None` is an expected value, so the handoff round-trip is broken for that input: a server with no `called_from` comes back from a re-exec believing it was launched from a file named `None`, and any consumer testing `called_from() is None` (or trying to open/exec that path) gets a wrong, non-existent path. Write `None` as `None` (e.g. `str(srv.called_from) if srv.called_from else None`) so the guard can do its job.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp_upgrade.py `execute()`

chunk_findings.detail: The final end-to-end assertion depends on the *old* process winning a race against the test's second write. The server only re-execs when it loops back and observes that stdin is idle (`test_serve_only_replaces_itself_when_quiet` proves queued requests are served *before* the exec). The test, however, cannot write request `id: 3` until it has read response `id: 2`; once that byte is flushed by the old server, the test process (on another core) can complete `json.loads` + `json.dumps` + `write` and enqueue the third request before the server reaches its `idle()` check. On that interleaving the old process serves request 3 itself, and per `test_reexec_flags_the_server_after_a_read_and_says_nothing` it emits no "restart the server" text, so `assert [c for c in second if "restart the server" in c["text"]]` fails even though the fix works. Nothing in the test synchronizes "server has re-execed" before the second `ask`, so the pass/fail depends on scheduling.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_on_upgrade.py::test_a_real_server_replaces_itself_on_the_same_stdio

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture clears `mcp_upgrade.HANDOFF_ENV` but never clears the mode variable `DDFLOW_MCP_ON_UPGRADE`, while three tests (`test_notify_never_re_execs`, `test_a_write_on_a_stale_server_says_reconnect_not_upgrade`, `test_reads_keep_working_on_a_stale_server`) assert *default-mode* behavior without setting it. Given `DDFLOW_MCP_ON_UPGRADE=reexec` in the ambient environment, `Server(stale).reexec_pending` becomes `True` and `test_notify_never_re_execs` fails; given `=off`, `test_a_write_on_a_stale_server_says_reconnect_not_upgrade` fails because the refusal no longer carries `restart_required`. The subprocess test is likewise affected because it launches with `env={**os.environ, ...}`, so an exported mode var overrides the `[mcp] on_upgrade = "reexec"` config the test just wrote.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_on_upgrade.py::stale (fixture)

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor adds `stale_facts` specifically to expose `reexec` — "the installed package is newer than the running code, so replacing the process would change something" — and the same change's `refusal()` relies on that flag (`if f is None or not f["reexec"]: return None`, "nothing newer is installed: a restart would not help"). `stale_server_note`, however, throws the flag away: it returns the "restart the server … to pick up the upgrade" message whenever `stale_facts` is non-`None`. Concrete input: `stale_facts(st, running="0.2.1", installed="0.2.1")` when the project log's highest stamp is `"0.2.3"` (written by a different checkout, so nothing newer than 0.2.1 is installed in this environment) yields `{"running": "0.2.1", "newest": "0.2.3", "where": "this project's log", "reexec": False}`, and `stale_server_note` then returns "note: this ddflow MCP server is running 0.2.1, but this project's log is at 0.2.3: restart the server (reconnect the MCP server in your client) to pick up the upgrade." Reconnecting re-launches the same installed 0.2.1 code, so the skew and the refusal persist — the agent is handed a fix that cannot work, which is exactly the failure mode the bug asks to eliminate. This is the same defect previously reported as finding 1 (`footer()` never consults `f["reexec"]`); the part of the change shown here does not answer it, because the note path itself still ignores the newly computed `reexec` flag, so any note/footer text derived from this function still adopts restart advice in the `reexec == False` case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_notice.py `stale_server_note` (new body)

chunk_findings.detail: The change keeps emitting the stale-server note from `footer()` on the ordinary reply path (it is appended verbatim into `out["content"]`) while the re-exec decision is only consulted on the refusal path (`_upgrade.refusal(self, exc)`). The triage is still `untriaged`, and nothing in this hunk conditions `footer()`'s note on `reexec`; the only new thing on this path is that `reexec_pending` may ask `serve` to replace the process, which does not affect what the *note* says. Concrete input: a server running 0.2.1 whose project log was stamped by 0.2.3 but where nothing newer than 0.2.1 is installed on disk (the writer used a different checkout/venv). `stale_server_facts` returns a non-`None` dict with `reexec == False`, `refusal()` correctly stays silent ("a restart would not help"), but `footer()` still tells the caller to "restart the server" — advice that cannot change anything and reproduces exactly the "one-line fix that is a trap" the bug is about.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py `_upgrade.footer(self)` (success-path footer loop, ~line 935) / `mcp_upgrade.footer`

chunk_findings.detail: `serve(repo, called_from=None)` is a legal call (the `Path | None` type of `called_from`), and this change now actually performs the handoff (`_upgrade.execute(srv)`), so the serialisation round-trip matters. `execute()` still writes `"called_from": str(srv.called_from)`, so for a server with no declared caller the handoff environment carries the literal `"None"`; the child's `called_from()` does `Path(value) if value else None`, `"None"` is truthy, so the re-exec'd process comes up with `called_from = Path("None")` instead of `None`. Every subsequent caller-attribution/telemetry decision in the new process then uses a bogus relative path. No serialisation fix is present in this diff and the finding is still untriaged.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py `serve` -> `_upgrade.execute(srv)` / `mcp_upgrade.execute`

chunk_findings.detail: Still holds (untriaged): the end-to-end assertion depends on the old process observing idle stdin and executing `_upgrade.execute` before the test's next request lands. The server only replaces itself after it has replied and looped back to `_reexec_ready(inp, relays)`, and the test cannot write `id: 3` until it has read `id: 2`; once `id: 2` is flushed the test process can run `json.loads`/`json.dumps`/`write` and have the bytes in the pipe before the server's idle check, in which case the request is served by the old code and the final assertion fails. The new code does not remove this ordering dependency (no synchronisation with the server's idle observation).
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_on_upgrade.py::test_a_real_server_replaces_itself_on_the_same_stdio

chunk_findings.detail: Still holds (untriaged): the fixture clears `mcp_upgrade.HANDOFF_ENV` but not the mode variable `DDFLOW_MCP_ON_UPGRADE`, while `test_notify_never_re_execs`, `test_a_write_on_a_stale_server_says_reconnect_not_upgrade` and `test_reads_keep_working_on_a_stale_server` assert default-mode behaviour without setting it. Run the suite with `DDFLOW_MCP_ON_UPGRADE=reexec` in the ambient environment and `Server(stale).reexec_pending` becomes `True`, so those default-mode assertions fail; with `=off` the stale-write/reconnect assertions take the other branch. The change adds the mode-driven `reexec_pending` field but does not isolate that variable in the fixture.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_on_upgrade.py::stale (fixture)

chunk_findings.detail: The `or start` reads as a safety net for a missing handoff value, but it can never fire for the one case where the handoff value is effectively absent. `execute()` serialises the caller with `"called_from": str(srv.called_from)`, so a server whose original `srv.called_from` was `None` writes the literal string `"None"`; `called_from()` then decodes `Path(value) if value else None`, and `"None"` is truthy, so it returns `Path("None")`. Given that input — launch the MCP server with no caller (a `None` `called_from`), let it re-exec on an upgrade — the re-exec'd process evaluates `_upgrade.called_from()` to `Path("None")`, which is truthy, so `or start` does not substitute the actual `start`, and the reassembled server advertises a bogus caller path (which is what feeds worktree adoption) instead of the fresh/absent one. The comment/guard added here does not answer the earlier round-trip finding, because the fix has to be on the write side (`execute()` emitting `null`/omitting the key, or `called_from()` treating the literal `"None"` as absent); no `or` fallback on the consumer can recover a value that was already corrupted to truthy garbage. This is the same root defect as the previously reported `execute()` round-trip issue, still present in the code this line depends on.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:1591 (`serve(repo, called_from=_upgrade.called_from() or start)`)

chunk_findings.detail: `footer()` still emits the restart note without ever consulting `f["reexec"]`, whereas `refusal()` guards on it (`if f is None or not f["reexec"]: return None`). The diff adds `test_no_restart_note_when_nothing_newer_is_installed`, but that is only an assertion of the desired behaviour; no code change to `footer()` is present. With running code 0.2.1, a project log stamped `99.0.0`, and `installed_version()` returning `"0.0.1"` (nothing newer installed), `stale_server_facts` yields a dict with `reexec == False`; a read (`ddflow_status`) will nevertheless carry the "restart the MCP server" note even though a restart would run exactly the same code — the note is unactionable and the new test that pins this case would fail.

chunk_findings.detail: The new early return feeds `mcp_upgrade.refusal(...)`'s value straight into `_ok(mid, stale)` and gates it with `is not None`. Every other helper in this file that produces a note (`footer`, `_obligation_footer`, and the removed `_stale_footer`, whose docstring ends "else ''") returns a plain note string and uses "" as the "nothing to say" sentinel; `footer` is consumed with truthiness (`if note:`). If `refusal` follows that same convention (plain string, "" or the raw `str(exc)` when the refusal is not a code-skew refusal), then the `is not None` test accepts the falsy/plain value: for any REFUSED exit that is not a version-skew refusal the branch returns `_ok(mid, stale)` — i.e. a JSON-RPC *success* whose result is an empty string / the bare refusal text — and the previous `meta={"exit": REFUSED}` marker (and any `isError`) is gone. Concrete failure: two agents race, agent A already holds the task, agent B calls `ddflow_claim`; the handler raises the claim-refused exception (`exit_for(exc) == REFUSED`); `refusal` returns "" (not `None`), `"" is not None` is True, so B receives `_ok(mid, "")` instead of the refusal text. Because the response now looks like a normal successful tool result with no `exit: REFUSED` marker, B treats the claim as granted and proceeds to write the task, producing exactly the conflicting-claim behavior the old code's `meta={"exit": REFUSED}` prevented. The same applies if `refusal` returns the note string directly rather than a pre-built CallToolResult: `_ok` expects the `_text(...)` result object, so the marker/error shape is silently dropped on this path.

chunk_findings.detail: When the running MCP server is stale and a write (`ddflow_claim`) is refused, the handler raises `SkewRefused`; `refusal()` turns that into the tool result `{"content": [...], "isError": False, "_meta": ...}`. Marking the refused call `isError: False` reports it to the client as a *successful* tool call. MCP clients and agent loops branch on `isError` to know a tool failed (to retry, surface the failure, or stop), so a refused claim now looks like a completed write: an agent that trusts the flag can proceed as if the claim/record was persisted — the exact "writing from here could drop what the newer one recorded" hazard the change is about, and the opposite of "reports the skew ... instead of leaving agents to fall back". The `REFUSED:` text and `_meta.exit = 3` are not a substitute for the protocol-level error bit, because the harness logic that the flag drives never gets to inspect the body. A refusal result from a staleness-aware rewrite must keep `isError: True` (only the wording should change).
